notes: Speaks at length with generally clear progression; some flexibility, occasional errors.
text: I would like to talk about a teacher who influenced me a lot. Her name was Mrs Karim and she taught me physics when I was about sixteen. Before her class, honestly, I thought physics was just a lot of formulas that you had to memorise for the exam, and I was not really interested in it at all. What made her different was that she never started with the equation. She would always start with a question, something ordinary, like why a heavy ball and a light ball fall at the same speed, and she would let us argue about it for ten minutes before she told us anything. Sometimes she would even let us stay wrong until the next lesson, which was frustrating, but it meant we actually thought about it. She also spent a lot of time with the students who were struggling. I remember she stayed after school twice a week without being paid for it. Because of her, I ended up choosing science for my degree, which I had not planned before. So I would say she changed the direction of my life, not just my marks in one subject.

notes: Fluent with only occasional self-correction; flexible and precise language; develops ideas fully.
text: I think the relationship between technology and traditional skills is more complicated than it is usually presented. The common assumption is that technology simply replaces older skills and that something valuable is lost, but I would argue the picture is more mixed than that. Take navigation as an example. It is certainly true that most people can no longer read a paper map properly, and that is a genuine loss in situations where the signal disappears. On the other hand, satellite navigation has made it possible for people to travel confidently to places they would never have attempted before, so access has widened even as one particular skill has narrowed. What concerns me more is not the disappearance of individual skills but the loss of the underlying judgement. If you have never navigated without assistance, you have no instinct for when the instructions you are being given are obviously wrong, and that is much harder to recover than the skill itself. So if I were designing an education system, I would not insist that children learn every traditional method for its own sake. I would focus on making sure they understand enough of the principle to notice when the tool is failing them.

notes: Fluent and precise throughout; idiomatic and well-controlled; ideas developed with nuance.
text: Whether governments should intervene in what people eat is one of those questions where the principle and the evidence pull in opposite directions, and I think it is worth being honest about that tension rather than pretending it does not exist. The libertarian objection is perfectly coherent: adults are entitled to make choices that harm only themselves, and a state that starts regulating diet has no obvious stopping point. What weakens that argument in practice is that the choices are rarely as free as the objection assumes. If the cheapest and most heavily advertised food available in a low-income neighbourhood is also the least nutritious, then describing the outcome as a free choice is doing a lot of work that the facts do not really support. That said, I am sceptical of the more heavy-handed interventions. Taxes on sugary drinks have produced measurable reductions in consumption, which is genuinely encouraging, but they also fall hardest on the people with the least disposable income, so you are effectively taxing poverty in order to address a problem that poverty largely caused. I would rather see governments intervene further upstream, on what gets subsidised, what can be marketed to children, and what is available in schools and hospitals, because those are decisions the state is already making. Adjusting choices the government has already shaped seems to me far easier to justify than restricting what an individual is permitted to buy.
